subtype: Approach: measuring use before changing it [Thinking]
passage: Counsellor's note, Monday. Ehsan brought his phone and showed me the weekly report he had found himself: six hours a day, most of it short videos. “I thought it was two,” he said. Then, after a silence, “I'm not going to feel bad about it. I'm going to plan from these numbers.” Together we looked at when the hours happen: on the bus after school and after dinner. He chose to trim only the after-dinner block by an hour for now, and to check the report again on Sunday. His mother, Himani, rang and asked what she could do. I suggested she ask Ehsan about the plan, and not check the phone behind his back. We will look at the numbers again in two weeks. — Nazia

qa.q: How many hours a day did the report show?
qa.a: Six hours a day, mostly short videos.

qa.q: How did Ehsan feel on seeing the number, and what did he decide?
qa.a: Shocked, since he had thought it was two hours, but he decided to use the numbers for a plan instead of feeling guilty.

qa.q: What else could Ehsan do to understand his habit, and why?
qa.a: Note what he was feeling just before scrolling, since knowing the trigger helps him choose a replacement.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Himani?
qa.a: Himani is worried and wants to help, so being told to ask about the plan instead of checking the phone gives her a role that keeps trust.

grounding: A teen checks his screen-time report, is shocked by six hours a day and decides to plan from real numbers instead of guilt.

subtype: Approach: asking what need the phone is meeting [Thinking]
passage: Dear Rekha, you asked why I've been so tired lately. I did something new: I asked myself why I scroll at night. I wrote down the honest answers on paper. One: it's lonely after everyone goes to bed, and the phone feels like company. Two: I'm dodging the maths homework because it makes my stomach tight. Neither is really about videos. So I made a plan with real replacements. On Thursdays I'd like to phone a friend at nine, and I was hoping that friend might be you. And I'll begin homework in ten-minute pieces, just ten, then a break. Would you mind being my nine o'clock call? I'll understand if not. — Vasudha

qa.q: What two things did Vasudha find behind the night scrolling?
qa.a: Loneliness after everyone goes to bed and dodging the maths homework.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel about this discovery?
qa.a: A mix of relief and sadness: naming the loneliness explained the scrolling and made a plan easier to write.

qa.q: What else could Vasudha try, and why?
qa.a: Start with a ten-minute homework goal at a fixed time, since a small start lowers the dread that sends Vasudha to the phone.

qa.q: How does the request look to Rekha?
qa.a: Rekha may feel touched and trusted, though Rekha will also need to decide whether that time can be given every Thursday.

grounding: A student asks why the scrolling happens at night, sees loneliness and homework worry, and plans real replacements.

subtype: Approach: if-then rules and phone-free zones [Action]
passage: Amandeep shared a bedroom and a small flat with his sister Sunaina, and the exam was eleven days away. He wrote two rules on a card: IF I open my books, THEN the phone goes on the hall shelf. IF the clock passes ten, THEN it spends the night out in the passage. On day two the phone buzzed from the shelf. He stood in the doorway staring at it. Sunaina, doing her own revision, said, “Want me to hide the charger?” “No. The rule is the rule.” He went back to the desk, jaw tight. On the fifth night he noticed he had not looked at the shelf once. The card curled at the corners, still pinned above the desk.

qa.q: Where does the phone go when Amandeep opens the books?
qa.a: On the hall shelf.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when the phone buzzed on day two?
qa.a: Tempted and restless: he stood staring at it, but held to his rule.

qa.q: What else could Amandeep add to the plan, and why?
qa.a: Set a fixed time to check messages after studying, since knowing when he can reply lowers the pull.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Sunaina?
qa.a: Sunaina, who shares the room, sees him tempted and offers help, and may feel relieved that he keeps to the rule himself and she does not have to police him.

grounding: A teen makes if-then rules and a phone-free study zone, so the choice becomes automatic.

subtype: Approach: app limits and removing triggers [Action]
passage:
Sunday. Lavanya sat on her bed with her phone and deleted the short-video apps one by one. She capped messaging at a fixed time each day, turned off every notification that wasn't from family, and moved her games to the computer in the hall, where she'd need to walk over and choose them.
Wednesday. At nine in the evening her thumb reached for the phone by itself. There was nothing to open. She felt restless and a bit bored. She texted her brother Rafiq: “bored.” He replied, “Come play carrom.” She did.
Sunday again. Homework had been finished before dinner three days in a row. The weekly report showed a lot fewer hours, and she looked at the number for a while.

qa.q: Which apps did Lavanya delete?
qa.a: The short-video apps.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling on Wednesday at nine?
qa.a: Restless and a bit bored: her thumb reached for the phone and there was nothing to open.

qa.q: What else could Lavanya do if the urge stays strong, and why?
qa.a: Plan something to do at that hour every evening, since removing the apps leaves a gap that something else needs to fill.

qa.q: How does Wednesday's text look to Rafiq?
qa.a: Rafiq gets a one-word message from his sister and offers something to do together, and may feel needed and glad to help.

grounding: A student deletes short-video apps, limits messaging, mutes notifications and moves games to a computer.

subtype: Approach: replacing the habit with an appealing alternative [Action]
passage: I'm Lokesh, and I live across the lane from Dolma. Every evening for months I saw Dolma on the front steps, scrolling, head bent, not even looking up when the ball rolled past. Then something changed. Last month I saw Dolma at the end of the lane with a borrowed bat, asking if there was room in our neighbourhood cricket game. At half past five each day since, there's been a figure in the field, chasing badly at first. And on Saturday mornings I've seen Dolma leave with a guitar case. I don't know if Dolma misses the phone. But the front steps are empty in the evenings now, and I've heard Dolma laughing.

qa.q: What two activities did Dolma sign up for?
qa.a: Evening cricket and a Saturday guitar class.

qa.q: What might Dolma have been feeling about the empty hours before joining?
qa.a: Bored and restless, though Lokesh can only guess; the scrolling on the steps and the later laughter hint at a change.

qa.q: What else could help Dolma stay with the new habits, and why?
qa.a: Invite a friend to join the guitar class, since company makes new routines easier to keep.

qa.q: How does the change look to Lokesh?
qa.a: Lokesh, who plays in the lane, gains a new player and sees the steps empty, and is glad to hear laughter even without knowing what Dolma felt.

grounding: A teen signs up for evening cricket and a weekend guitar class so the free hours are filled.

subtype: Approach: cold-turkey resolution announced on the first day [Pitfall]
passage: On the first of the month, Tomas announced at dinner in Lisbon: no screens for thirty days. Phone, tablet, everything. He deleted every app, even the messaging one. On day three the class trip changed to an earlier bus, and everyone knew except Tomas, because the school group ran on messaging. Clara, a classmate, found him at the gate and said, “Didn't you see? We moved the time.” On day four, hurt and tired of being out of the loop, Tomas borrowed a phone “just once” and scrolled for three hours. “I've failed,” he said that night. “So forget it.” By the weekend he was back to every old habit, more than before. All or nothing, and the nothing had lasted four days.

qa.q: On which day did Tomas break his rule?
qa.a: Day four.

qa.q: How did Tomas feel after breaking the rule?
qa.a: Disappointed and discouraged: he said he had failed and gave up on the whole plan.

qa.q: What alternative could have worked better, and why?
qa.a: Limiting the short videos and games but keeping the school messaging, since a rule that fits real life is easier to keep.

qa.q: How does Tomas's plan look to Clara?
qa.a: Clara sees a rule that was too strict for how school works, and probably wishes Tomas had kept the useful part instead of giving up everything.

grounding: A student swears off all screens for a month, ignores that school groups run on messaging, breaks the rule by day four and quits the effort.

subtype: Approach: promising to start on Monday [Pitfall]
passage: Dear Rajni Masi, you asked how my plan to cut down my phone time is going. I'm embarrassed to say it hasn't started. Not truly. First I said I'd start after the festival. Then I said after the unit tests. Then Monday, because Mondays are for beginnings. Then the next Monday, because that Monday was a bad one. Each time the reason sounds good to me, and each time I check the report and the hours are the same, five or six a day. I can see that the better start date keeps moving, like the horizon. I keep making the promise because it feels good to make it. I'm writing to you so that it is on paper. Love, Pradeep

qa.q: What reasons did Pradeep give for postponing the plan?
qa.a: After the festival, after the unit tests, and next Monday.

qa.q: How does Pradeep feel writing to Rajni Masi?
qa.a: Embarrassed and a bit trapped: the promises feel good to make but nothing has changed.

qa.q: What could Pradeep do instead of waiting for a better date, and why?
qa.a: Start today with one small change, since waiting for a perfect start date is what keeps the habit going.

qa.q: How does the delay look to Rajni Masi?
qa.a: Rajni Masi sees repeated promises with no change, and may be worried but also relieved that Pradeep is being honest.

grounding: A teen keeps delaying a plan to a better start date, so the habit continues unchanged for months.

subtype: Approach: agreeing family rules together rather than imposed ones [Action]
passage:
“Here's my idea,” Kamal said at dinner, placing his phone face down. “Devices off during meals, and off after ten. For everyone.”
His mother Zainab stopped mid-bite. “Everyone?”
“Everyone. You and Papa too.”
Papa laughed. “Even my cricket scores?”
“Even your cricket scores.”
Zainab put down her fork. “I check messages during dinner without thinking. So I'd be changing too.”
“That's the point,” Kamal said. “If only I do it, it feels like a punishment. If we all do it, it's just how our house works.”
Papa looked at Zainab. “Fair.” “Fair,” she said. “We try it for a month, then decide.”
Kamal grinned and slid the phones into the basket by the door.

qa.q: At what time do the devices go off each night?
qa.a: After ten.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel when his mother agrees to follow the rule as well?
qa.a: Surprised and respected: he expected a fight and instead found the family agreeing.

qa.q: What else could the family do to keep the rule going, and why?
qa.a: Review it after the month and adjust it together, since a rule everyone shaped is easier to keep.

qa.q: How does the rule look to Zainab?
qa.a: Zainab realises she checks messages at dinner without thinking, so she finds the rule fair though it also means giving up her own habit.

grounding: A teen and parents agree devices are off at meals and after ten, with parents following the same rule.

passage: Sunday, late. I slipped this weekend. Saturday and most of Sunday went on videos, and I feel low about it. But I've decided not to be horrible to myself, because that never helped. Instead I asked what set it off. First there was the argument with my brother on Friday, which left me angry and restless. Then there was nothing planned, so the empty hours filled up. That's two triggers: a fight and boredom. So here's what changes: next Saturday I've asked my friend Keerthana to go to the market with me, something fixed and outside. And tomorrow I start again as normal. One bad weekend doesn't cancel the two good weeks. — Rekha

qa.q: What set off the weekend of videos?
qa.a: An argument with a brother and having nothing planned.

qa.q: How does Rekha feel about the slip, and how is it handled?
qa.a: Low and disappointed, but Rekha chooses to be kind to self instead of harsh, and looks for triggers.

qa.q: What else could Rekha do to prepare for boring stretches, and why?
qa.a: Keep a short list of things to do when bored, since a ready list is easier to use than deciding on the spot.

qa.q: How does the outing look to Keerthana?
qa.a: Keerthana, invited to the market, may feel glad to be included and to help a friend get through a hard weekend.

grounding: After a weekend slip, a student checks the triggers, plans an outing for next weekend and restarts the next day.

subtype: Approach: seeking help when control keeps failing [Revision]
passage:
Weeks one to four. Yash tried everything: app limits, the phone on the hall shelf, if-then cards. Each plan worked for a few days. Then he was scrolling till two in the morning again. His marks slid from seventy-two to fifty-eight. He felt ashamed and told nobody.
Week five. After a bad exam he said to his mother, “I've tried and I can't stop.” She didn't scold. The next morning they both went to see Trisha ma'am, the school counsellor.
Two weeks later. Trisha ma'am had set up a structured routine with Yash, with fixed wind-down time and a weekly check-in. “If it keeps going or worries you, we can look at more support together,” she said. That night Yash was asleep by eleven.

qa.q: Who did Yash speak to, with his parent?
qa.a: Trisha ma'am, the school counsellor.

qa.q: How did Yash feel after several failed plans?
qa.a: Ashamed and frustrated: he told nobody and only spoke after a bad exam.

qa.q: What else could Yash do if the routine is not enough, and why?
qa.a: Tell the counsellor and his parents so they can look at more support, since needing more help is a sign to ask, not a failure.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Trisha ma'am?
qa.a: Trisha ma'am sees a student who kept trying and then asked for help, and can offer a routine and follow-up with his parents without blame.

grounding: Despite several plans, a teen still loses sleep and grades, and speaks to a school counsellor with a parent.
